analysis.one_liner: Restores federal preapproval of election changes in states with recent voting-rights violations.
analysis.headline: A voting-rights bill with 220 Democratic cosponsors — enough to pass the House on paper — has sat untouched in the House Judiciary Committee since its introduction on March 5, 2025.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would bring back "preclearance": states and counties with recent records of voting-rights violations would need approval from the Justice Department or a federal court before changing their election rules. It also spells out how courts should judge claims that district maps or voting rules dilute or burden minority voters, requires governments to publicly announce voting changes and polling-place staffing, and gives the Justice Department new power to demand documents during voting-rights investigations.
analysis.who_benefits: Voters — especially Black, Hispanic, Asian, Native American, and language-minority voters — who live in jurisdictions with recent voting-rights violations. Preclearance would stop discriminatory maps and rules before they take effect, instead of after an election has been run under them. All voters gain from required public notice when voting rules or polling places change.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Voters in jurisdictions with violation records

how_it_helps.text: Restores preclearance using a new formula: a state is covered for 10 years if it had 15 or more voting-rights violations in the past 25 years, 10 or more with at least one by the state itself, or 3 or more where the state runs the elections; a county or city is covered separately after 3 violations.

Requires preapproval not just for entire covered states but for specific practices — such as switching to at-large elections, cutting multilingual ballots, consolidating polling places, tightening voter ID, or redistricting in areas with large minority populations.
Gives courts a defined test for vote dilution and vote denial claims, so plaintiffs challenging maps or rules like strict photo ID laws have clearer legal standards.
Requires states and large localities to publicly post changes to voting rules within 48 hours, and to publish polling-place locations, hours, machines, and staffing before federal elections.
Allows the Justice Department to demand relevant documents from states and localities before filing a voting-rights lawsuit, and lets both the Department and individual voters sue to enforce the law.
Includes an exit path: covered political subdivisions that have kept a clean record for ten years can apply for an exemption, and coverage expires after ten years unless new violations occur.

analysis.who_pays: State and local election offices in covered jurisdictions, which must get federal approval before making many election changes, publish detailed public notices, and respond to Justice Department document demands. State legislatures also give up some control over how they draw districts and write election rules.
analysis.who_pays_short: Covered state and local election offices

drawbacks.text: Preclearance means a covered state or county cannot put a new election rule in place until the Justice Department approves it or a federal court signs off — a federal check on state control of elections that critics call an overreach and that the Supreme Court struck down in its old form in 2013.

The coverage formula looks back 25 years, so states can be covered in part for violations that occurred under laws and maps from decades ago, and the bill applies its new retrogression rule to actions taken since 2021.

The bill adds litigation risk both ways: jurisdictions face preclearance and injunctions, while plaintiffs gain a broader definition of discriminatory burden that could reach voting rules defended as ordinary election administration.
Covered jurisdictions bear real administrative costs — preapproval submissions, 48-hour public notices, and detailed polling-place reporting.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core benefit is concrete: voters in places with repeated voting-rights violations get a system that screens discriminatory changes before elections, rather than years-long lawsuits afterward. The costs are real but narrower — compliance work for election offices and a loss of discretion for covered states. The design includes softeners (a ten-year coverage window, an exemption process for clean jurisdictions, and automatic coverage only after repeated violations). The main legitimate objection is constitutional and philosophical: it re-establishes federal control over election rulemaking in some states, a power the Supreme Court rejected in its previous form in 2013, and a future court fight over the new formula is likely. On balance, the bill's benefits flow to ordinary voters and its costs to governments with records of violations.

outcome.mechanism: Introduced March 5, 2025 and referred to the House Judiciary Committee, which has taken no action — no hearing, no committee vote — and the bill has never reached the House floor.

narrative.text: Rep. Terri Sewell introduced the John R. Lewis Voting Rights Advancement Act of 2025 on March 5, 2025, and it was referred to the House Committee on the Judiciary.
The bill attracted 220 cosponsors, all of them Democrats, within days of introduction.
Since the referral, the action history shows no further steps — no hearing, no markup, no committee vote, and no floor action.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Incumbent state legislators, map-drawers, and election officials in covered jurisdictions are better off, because the bill stalled before it could require federal preapproval of redistricting and election-rule changes.

for.name: Rep. Terri Sewell
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and assembled 220 original cosponsors, positioning it as the successor to the Voting Rights Act's struck-down coverage formula.

for.name: 220 House Democrats
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, including the party's House leadership; the cosponsor count includes non-voting delegates such as the representatives of DC and the Virgin Islands.

against.name: House Judiciary Committee
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on referral on March 5, 2025 and has taken no action on it since — no hearing, no markup, no vote.

against.name: Rep. Jim Jordan
against.what_they_did: Has not scheduled the bill for a committee hearing or vote.

against.name: Rep. Mike Johnson
against.what_they_did: Has not brought the bill to the House floor for a vote despite its majority-size cosponsor list.

sides.party_line_note: All 220 cosponsors are Democrats and no Republican has signed on; the Republican House majority has not moved the bill at any stage.

industries.industry: State legislatures and other incumbent map-drawers
industries.note: The bill would subject redistricting in covered, diverse jurisdictions to federal preapproval and give courts a test for racial vote dilution, constraining the ability of officeholders to draw maps favoring themselves and their party. Because those same officeholders set the legislative agenda, the people whose power the bill would limit are the ones deciding whether it moves.

Covered jurisdictions would face compliance costs — preapproval submissions, 48-hour public notices, detailed polling-place reporting — but would gain a clear legal safe harbor once a practice is precleared, rather than facing lawsuits after elections are run.

industries.industry: Election-law litigators and voting-rights advocacy groups
industries.note: The bill creates new causes of action, clearer standards, and a Justice Department document-demand tool, expanding the work of enforcing voting rights — an interest that runs alongside voters' ability to challenge discriminatory rules.

analysis.trajectory: With Republicans holding 223 House seats and the Judiciary chair controlling whether the bill ever gets a hearing, it is very unlikely to receive a committee vote or floor action in this Congress; a version of the bill passed the House only in 2021, when Democrats held the majority. Its realistic path is reintroduction in a future Congress with different chamber control.
